input.question: Why is it bad to reuse water bottles when unopened bottles can sit on the shelf indefinitely?
input.ground_truth: Manufacturing student here who works with plastics all the time. Most water bottles are made out of PET (poly ethylene terephthalate). Inherently, PET has nothing in it that could cause cancer etc, but the additives that the manufacturer uses can. They will add things like color, UV additives, fillers etc and these are the things that are actually harmful. BPA comes from only certain plastics like polycarbonate and PEEK (poly ether-ether ketone) and most companies will not uses these plastics in food or beverage containers. According to what I've learned, unless the plastic is melting in your food/drink, its generally safe and not "leeching chemicals" like everyone thinks. As far as bacteria goes, I don't know much about that to be honest

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why is it bad to reuse water bottles when unopened bottles can sit on the shelf indefinitely?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big, clean water bottle that’s still sealed and hasn’t been opened yet. That bottle is super clean and safe to drink from because nothing has touched the inside.

But if you use a water bottle, drink from it, and then use it again without washing it really, really well, tiny germs can hide in places you can’t see. These germs can make you sick if you drink from the bottle again.

Now, unopened bottles on the shelf are like brand new toys that nobody has played with yet—they stay clean and safe because nobody touched them.

But once you open a bottle and use it, it’s like you played with your toy and now it needs to be cleaned before you play with it again, or you might get germs on your hands.

So, reusing a water bottle without cleaning it is bad because it can make you sick with germs, but unopened bottles are still perfectly clean and safe to use anytime!
